source.title: The Importance of Prompt Tuning for Automated Neuron Explanations
source.authors: Justin Lee; Tuomas P. Oikarinen; Arjun Chatha; Keng-Chi Chang; Yilan Chen; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates automated neuron explanations by simulating their predicted activations and comparing them with actual activations, but varies the explanation prompts rather than reproducing the claimed audit.
record.gate_note: The simulation scores in Table 2 bear on V7. The paper does not report how many individual neurons pass a stated threshold for a good score, so the reported averages cannot establish the claimed minority share. The explanation-fit versus held-out firing comparison required by V6 is not reported. Prompt token counts, AdaCS similarities, human ratings, and puzzle results are not rows because they do not measure prediction of activations on new text.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own simulate-and-score evaluation of neuron explanations on unseen text for random GPT-2 XL MLP neurons, with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 explainers and five prompts. It bears on V7, but uses GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct as simulator instead of GPT-4 and reports only mean scores.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that simpler prompts, especially Summary, improve explanation quality at 2–3× lower cost. Gains are large with GPT-3.5 and differences shrink with GPT-4. They make no claim about the overall share of well-explained neurons, beyond restating the original work's point that most neurons are poorly explained.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the original neuron-explanation pipeline and simulate-and-score evaluation on GPT-2(XL), but tests alternate explanation prompts; the study does not reproduce the original audit-share measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt format and explainer model affect scores. The authors report GPT-3.5 results favor Summary, whereas GPT-4 results are more similar across prompts; selecting neurons with high scores under the Original prompt biases the random-interpretable comparison.
record.problems: The study evaluates subsets of GPT-2(XL) neurons rather than all neurons; it gives mean simulation scores but no distribution or threshold defining a good score. GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct, rather than GPT-4, is used as the simulator, and GPT-4 explanations are evaluated only at smaller scale. The authors also note selection bias in the random-interpretable subset.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the relevant simulation-score results in Table 2. Other prompt-length, AdaCS, puzzle-similarity, and human-rating results were excluded because they do not measure prediction of activations on unseen text.

untested.parts: No cross-model or scale audit of shares.
No architecture, regularization or vision-model comparison.
No comparison of fit on the explaining examples against held-out prediction.
No per-neuron score distribution or share above a good-score threshold for random neurons. The GPT-4 simulator setting is not used.

record.verdict_notes: Only the random-subset rows can speak to the population, and they report means rather than shares. The weaker simulator (GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct rather than GPT-4) may lower absolute scores relative to the original. The intro's 'vast majority' remark cites [2] and is not the study's own result. AdaCS, puzzle and human-rating results do not measure prediction of activations on new text and were rightly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares are not measured.
No cross-model or scale audit of the claimed shares is reported.
No InceptionV1 examples or recursive-generalization analysis.
No architecture, regularization, or vision-model interpretability-share comparison.
The study does not compare how well explanations fit the examples used to write them against how well they predict firing on held-out text.
Simulation scores on unseen text are reported, but the study gives neither a definition of a good score nor the fraction of neurons above such a threshold.

relationships.condition: Random GPT-2 XL MLP neurons; GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 explainer; all five prompts; GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct simulator
relationships.reason: Mean simulation scores stay about 0.10–0.12. The stronger GPT-4 explainer and better prompts raise them only slightly. Inferred from means, not shares (r1,r4,r7,r10,r13,r16,r19,r22,r25,r28).
relationships.display_finding: Mean simulation scores stayed around 0.10–0.12, and the stronger GPT-4 explainer and better prompts raised them only slightly. This is read from mean scores, not from the share of neurons that scored well.

source_check.reason: Random-neuron means are 0.0962-0.1249 (GPT-3.5) and 0.1193-0.1241 (GPT-4). They stay low with the stronger explainer and every prompt. Means only, no shares above a threshold.

relation.reason: Reports its own simulate-and-score results for random GPT-2 XL neurons, and these bear on V7.

tranche.reason: Runs its own simulate-and-score on the original GPT-2 XL setting, but with a different simulator (GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct) and means instead of shares, so T2 fits.

source_check.notes: Table 2 also gives Random Interpretable subsets (0.22-0.29), picked by NeuronViewer score >0.35, so they don't compare with the Random rows. On that subset GPT-3.5 beats GPT-4 for every prompt. GPT-3.5 used 20 neurons per layer and GPT-4 used 10. The intro only restates [2]'s point that most neurons are poorly explained.

statements.correction: Table 2, Random neurons, GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 explainer: Original 0.1211 vs 0.0962; Highlight 0.1241 vs 0.1129; AVHS 0.1219 vs 0.1093; Summary 0.1238 vs 0.1249; HS 0.1193 vs 0.1239. Random Interpretable: GPT-3.5 is higher for every prompt (Original 0.2420 vs 0.2284). Neuron samples differ: 20 per layer for GPT-3.5, 10 for GPT-4. Simulator: GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct.
statements.problem: 0.1211 vs 0.0962 is correct, but only for the Original prompt on Random neurons, and the subset isn't named. Citing it as evidence that stronger explainers raise scores leaves out that the study's other cells are mixed.
